title: The Use of a Smartphone EEG in Adults With Epilepsy
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Northwestern University; conditions: Epilepsy; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 1500; status: RECRUITING] In this prospective, open-label, single-arm, dual-institution trial, the investigators aim to develop a general-purpose AI able to identify epilepsy and type of epilepsy in EEG to facilitate the epilepsy diagnosis using smartphone EEG in resource-limited settings.

title: HapAdapter: A Transfer Learning Protocol for DNA Foundation Models Adapted to Diploid Personal Epigenomes
desc: The rapid rise of large language models (LLMs) has spurred the development of genomic language models (gLMs) that capitalize on the key features of natural language present in biological sequences. Moreover, DNA foundation models, a sub-class of gLMs, have demonstrated impressive accuracy in predicting a wide range of functional tracks from DNA sequence input. However, current DNA foundation models are exclusively trained on haploid reference genome sequences -- despite personal and graph genomes becoming the new standard for genomic analyses. This is principally because the cost to train gLMs on a personal diploid genome for a single individual is not currently practical. To help reconcile this disconnect between the current available use-cases of DNA foundation models with the modern direction of genomic sequence analysis, we present HapAdapter, a transfer-learning protocol that builds a small Siamese network on top of any pre-trained foundation model to enable inference from full diploid personal genome context. To demonstrate the utility of this method, we train a set of HapAdapter heads to predict allele-specific effects across assays on two representative foundation model backbones: DNABERT-2 and AlphaGenome. We demonstrate that our lightweight adapter more than doubles DNABERT-2's allele-specific discrimination and triples AlphaGenome's (130% and 210% gain in AUROC above chance, respectively, averaged over nine assays).

title: Digital transformation of neonatal neurocritical care: Integrating telemedicine, multimodal monitoring, and precision neuroprotection.
source: PubMed · Seminars in fetal & neonatal medicine
desc: [Seminars in fetal & neonatal medicine] Neonatal brain injury remains a major contributor to mortality and long-term neurodevelopmental disability worldwide. Over the past two decades, neonatal neurocritical care (NNCC) has emerged as an interdisciplinary model focused on early diagnosis, continuous neuromonitoring, and neuroprotective interventions. Digital health technologies are now accelerating this transformation by expanding access to specialized expertise, enabling remote neuromonitoring, and supporting more standardized and individualized care across geographically distributed neonatal intensive care units (NICUs). This review discusses the evolving roles of telemedicine, multimodal monitoring, immersive technologies, artificial intelligence, and digital data ecosystems in NNCC. We explore current clinical applications, implementation challenges, and future perspectives, including precision neuroprotection, predictive analysis, and longitudinal digital neuro-NICU models. By integrating these technologies, digitally connected NNCC may help shift the field from reactive treatment of established injury toward proactive, precision-based neuroprotection focused on lifelong brain health.

title: Capturing human expertise for AI-assisted molecular structure annotation
desc: We developed a large language model-based tool that captures expert reasoning in bile acid structure elucidation, drawing on hand written notebooks, scientific literature, and recorded voice-to-text analytical sessions. It generates human-readable reports detailing evidence for and against candidate structures, tracing each inference to its source and identifying ambiguities. When applied to data, the tool proposes bile acid conjugates lacking reference spectra.

title: External Validation of Stateless Large Language Model Data Extraction for Systematic Review Reconstruction.
source: PubMed · Methods of information in medicine
desc: [Methods of information in medicine] Objectives Large language models are increasingly used in evidence synthesis, but high accuracy among returned values may coexist with consequential omissions. We evaluated a stateless, source-grounded artificial intelligence (AI) workflow for extracting data from primary randomized-trial reports and reconstructing meta-analyses. Methods The fixed corpus comprised 15 randomized trials from a published review of regional anesthesia for pediatric cardiac surgery. For each trial report, one stateless extraction attempt was made with GPT-5.6-sol through the application programming interface (API), using the primary-report PDF and a frozen prompt and schema. No review material was supplied at inference time. A transport-only retry was permitted only when no scientific output had been produced. The reference standard was a manually source-verified universe of target-positive cells. Outcomes included composite reconstruction accuracy, precision, completeness, source support, rescue performance, and pooled-estimate reconstruction. Results Thirteen primary calls produced contract-valid outputs; two completed outputs failed the support contract. Of 1,657 evaluable cells, 821 satisfied the preregistered composite requirement for exact content and adequate source support (49.55%). Among 897 positive claims, 892 were content-exact (99.44%), 823 had adequate support (91.75%), and 821 met both criteria (protocol-composite precision 91.53%). Completeness was 54.13%, and 760 source-present cells were omitted. Effect direction agreed in all 11 syntheses estimable from both input sets, but only eight used the same study set; four of 15 source-based syntheses were not estimable from AI inputs. Both failed trials produced a valid first rescue output, with 173 of 284 cells exact and supported (60.92%). Conclusions Returned positive claims were usually content-exact, but only 91.53% met the full content-and-support criterion and the workflow recovered only about half of source-present cells. These findings support stateless extraction as human-verified assistance with explicit auditing of omissions and source support, rather than as autonomous systematic-review extraction.

title: A Benchmark for Generative Modeling of High-Dimensional Enzyme Kinetic Parameters of Metabolic Networks
desc: Large-scale kinetic models predict how metabolism responds to genetic and environmental perturbations, but building them at scale is limited by the scarcity of experimentally determined enzyme kinetic parameters. Generative machine learning has been proposed to address this bottleneck, yet prior work has each introduced a single, bespoke architecture, leaving open which generative paradigm suits this problem and why. We introduce a benchmark suite for generative modeling of high-dimensional enzyme kinetic parameter sets: labeled datasets of kinetically feasible Escherichia coli models paired with a mechanistically grounded evaluation harness that scores generated ensembles on dynamical stability and agreement with experimentally observed phenotypes, rather than statistical realism alone. Using it, we compare three standard architectures at matched capacity, a conditional variational autoencoder, a Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty, and a RealNVP normalizing flow, each under two conditioning schemes (a discrete high/low label and a continuous, graded key-performance-indicator target), across a difficulty ladder from one mutant phenotype to a stringent class of nine reproduced jointly. Two findings stand out. The architectures trace a consistent concentration-exploration trade-off, the VAE concentrating, the flow exploring and extrapolating, the GAN in between, but this ordering is overturned at high stringency by the conditioning scheme: at the joint class, continuous targets reach 33 to 117-fold enrichment over random sampling for every architecture, whereas discrete labels stay at 1.3 to 15-fold. Beyond the comparison, the suite is an accessible, mechanistically validated reference task for groups outside the kinetic-modeling community to benchmark their own generative algorithms.

title: The Completion-Verification Gap in Clinical Nurses' Integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence Into Nursing Work: A Qualitative Study.
desc: [Journal of clinical nursing] To explore how clinical nurses integrate generative artificial intelligence into nursing work, focusing on task support, perceived ability to verify outputs and professional responsibility. GenAI is increasingly used in nursing, but little is known about how nurses perceive their ability to verify outputs when task barriers are reduced, especially in evidence-sensitive or patient-related tasks. Between October and December 2025, a qualitative descriptive study was conducted in four tertiary hospitals in Nantong, China. Clinical nurses with experience of using GenAI were recruited using purposive maximum-variation sampling. Data were collected through individual semi-structured interviews and analysed using inductive thematic analysis. Data collection and analysis were conducted concurrently, with saturation assessed after 21 interviews and confirmed by one additional interview. Twenty-two clinical nurses were interviewed. Three themes and six subthemes were identified: (1) broadening GenAI use across nursing tasks, including progression from routine drafting to diverse nursing tasks and lowering task barriers; (2) the completion-verification gap, encompassing efficiency and learning support alongside superficial understanding and premature confidence; and (3) risk-calibrated integration, involving risk-based verification, retained professional responsibility and organisational safeguards. GenAI facilitated engagement with information-intensive and unfamiliar nursing tasks. However, easier task completion did not necessarily resolve perceived difficulties in identifying omissions, fabricated information or inappropriate recommendations. Safe integration therefore requires nurses to calibrate verification according to task risk, retain responsibility for final decisions and have access to organisational safeguards that support traceable and accountable use. Safe GenAI use in nursing requires risk-based verification, retained professional accountability and appropriate organisational safeguards. No patients or members of the public were involved because this study focused on clinical nurses' professional experiences.

title: rnaModScan: context-aware deep learning-based filtering of nanopore m6A and inosine calls
desc: Nanopore direct RNA sequencing (DRS) can detect multiple RNA modifications, but falsepositive background calls complicate transcriptome-wide analysis. We developed rnaModScan,a deep learning filter that integrates Dorado scores for all eight modification types with local sequence, repeat, and per-read alignment features to distinguish N6-methyladenosine (m6A) and inosine candidates from background calls. Using public RNA004 data, we evaluated site classification by grouped five-fold cross-validation and assessed transfer to HeLa cellular RNA using model weights fitted exclusively to HEK293T cellular RNA and unmodified in vitrotranscribed controls. For m6A sites outside the canonical DRACH motif, filtering removed 92.85% of the Dorado/modkit candidates while retaining 93.34% of their original matches to the GLORI reference map. The F1 score relative to DRS-covered GLORI sites increased from 3.04% to 26.76%. For inosine, filtering removed 83.44% of the candidates while preserving 99.86% of their original Slic-seq matches, and the reference-map F1 score increased from 5.22% to 22.05%. Filtering also brought the motif, repeat, and transcript-position distributions of retained candidates closer to those in the orthogonal short-read maps generated by GLORI and Slic-seq. These results support rnaModScan as a practical complement to Dorado-based RNA004 analysis for prioritizing transcriptome-wide m6A and inosine candidates.Availability: rnaModScan is available at https://github.com/uedaLabR/rnaModScan and archived in Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24546829).Keywords: direct RNA sequencing; RNA modifications; Dorado; deep learning; inosine; m6A

title: Artificial Intelligence, Motivation, and Burnout Among Radiologists and Radiation Oncologists.
source: PubMed · Journal of medical imaging and radiation oncology
desc: [Journal of medical imaging and radiation oncology] Burnout is a major concern across medical professions, with radiologists and radiation oncologists among the most affected. Artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to reduce burnout by decreasing workload; however, previous research has shown inconsistent associations between AI use and burnout. These relationships may depend on clinicians' motivation for using AI. A 6.5 min anonymous online survey was distributed to members of the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists (RANZCR) over a 2 month period (May-July 2025). Measures included demographics and work-related variables (hours, level of training), burnout, AI use (frequency and task type), and motivation to use AI (based on Self-Determination Theory). Motivation was examined as a moderator of the relationship between AI use and burnout. Responses were received from 121 clinicians (90 radiologists, 31 radiation oncologists), including 21 trainees. Clinically significant burnout was reported by 42.1% (51/121) of respondents. Ninety-one (75.2%) respondents reported using AI, primarily for image analysis and interpretation (radiologists) and treatment planning (radiation oncologists). There was no overall significant relationship between AI use and burnout. However, AI use was positively associated with burnout among those reporting lower autonomy in AI use. This relationship was not mediated by need satisfaction or frustration. AI use is common among RANZCR members, and the burnout rate is prevalent. These preliminary findings highlight the potential importance of supporting autonomous motivation when implementing AI, while recognising that larger and more context-specific studies are required to confirm this relationship.

title: Confident but misplaced: a model-free ruler for post-translational modification placement by AI structure predictors
desc: AI structure predictors accept post-translationally modified (PTM) residues, but whether they place the added atoms where crystallography finds them, and whether their confidence reveals when they do not, is unknown. We first built a ruler from experiment alone: independent crystal structures of the same site reproduce the added atoms of oxidised cysteine and methionine to 0.32 [A], the closest pre-cutoff library rotamer lies at 0.41 [A] and a model-free guess at 4.17 [A]. We then predicted 176 hold-out PTM sites, released after every model's training cut-off, with RareFold, Boltz-2, Chai-1 and AlphaFold 3, using identical inputs and thresholds fixed before measurement. On oxidised Cys/Met (up to 34 sites in 25 proteins), the three all-atom models place the matching distal atoms of neighbouring canonical side chains to 0.35-0.38 [A] but the added oxygens at 1.19-1.51 [A]; 29-41 % of placements are wrong by more than 2 [A], as sterically plausible rotamers that the electron density does not support. RareFold misplaces ordinary side chains as well. Across all PTM classes, residue confidence does not flag the failure: at pLDDT [≥] 90, 24-46 % of modified-residue placements are catastrophic, 3.5-5 times the rate for matched canonical atoms. One seed rarely samples the correct rotamer; more seeds sample it more often, yet the models' own ranking does not select it. Methyllysine shows the same gap, whereas for pyridoxal-lysine the models diverge (AlphaFold 3 1.13 [A], Boltz-2 4.96 [A]). A high residue pLDDT at a modified residue therefore does not verify its side chain.

title: Heart Rate Variability Estimation from 3D Seismocardiography: A Deep Learning Approach with a Large-Scale Dataset.
desc: [Physiological measurement] Heart rate variability (HRV) is a widely used non-invasive marker of autonomic nervous system regulation, with applications in stress assessment, recovery monitoring, and cardiovascular health evaluation. With the increasing use of wearable technologies, seismocardiography (SCG) has emerged as a promising modality for estimating resting HRV from cardiac mechanical activity. However, large-scale validation of deep learning-based HRV estimation from wearable triaxial SCG remains limited. This study aimed to develop and evaluate a deep learning-based framework for estimating HRV from triaxial SCG signals using a large-scale, real-world resting-state wearable dataset. A three-channel 1D U-Net was trained to detect heartbeat timing from short-term resting SCG recordings. The model was developed using data from over 5,500 subjects and evaluated on an independent test cohort of 940 individuals. Reference heartbeat timing was derived from ECG-based RR intervals and used to generate Gaussian target masks for model training. Inter-beat intervals (IBIs) estimated from SCG-derived beat timings were subsequently used to compute time-domain, frequency-domain, Poincaré plot, and non-linear HRV metrics. The proposed framework classified 93.8% of recordings as suitable for HRV analysis. For these, SCG-derived IBIs showed excellent agreement with reference RR intervals (r = 0.981, bias = 0.190 ms). Time-domain HRV metrics demonstrated strong correlations with reference values across recording effective durations of 30-300 s (r = 0.988-0.999), whereas frequency-domain and nonlinear HRV metrics, evaluated using recordings with an effective duration exceeding 120 s, also showed high correlations (r = 0.843-0.995). These findings demonstrate that HRV estimation from resting SCG is feasible at scale, with particularly strong performance for time-domain and Poincaré plot metrics. By achieving robust beat timing and HRV agreement in a real-world resting cohort, the proposed framework advances SCG as a practical non-invasive alternative or complement to ECG-based HRV monitoring.

title: Artificial intelligence (AI) in implant selection: an evaluation of AI-generated preoperative templating in total joint arthroplasty.
source: PubMed · European journal of orthopaedic surgery & traumatology : orthopedie traumatologie
desc: [European journal of orthopaedic surgery & traumatology : orthopedie traumatologie] Artificial intelligence (AI) applications have become widely accessible resources, and the race is on to determine the safe application of this technology within total joint arthroplasty (TJA). One area of investigation is the use of AI with in preoperative templating for total hip (THA) and total knee arthroplasty (TKA). This study aimed to compare the accordance of AI- and surgeon-generated templates to the implants utilized in consecutive TJA cases. A retrospective review was performed of 349 THA and 390 TKA cases from a single academic arthroplasty practice between March 2025 and October 2025. Preoperative radiographs were evaluated to produce AI- and surgeon-generated THA templates for cup and stem size, which were compared to components implanted. For TKA, AI-generated template was compared to implanted femoral, tibial, and patellar components. Analysis was performed using mixed-effects models with a random intercept for surgeons, with Holm-adjusted two-tailed significance set at α = 0.05. For THA, surgeon and AI-generated templates overestimated cup (p < 0.0001) and stem (p < 0.0001) size. Surgeon-templated stem sizes were utilized in 30.1% of cases, making surgeon more frequently accurate than AI (22.4%; p = 0.02). Surgeon and AI-templated cup sizes were utilized in 35.8% and 29.8% of cases, respectively, which was not a statistically significant difference (p = 0.09). Compared with the actual implants utilized in TKA, AI tended to oversize femoral, tibial, and patella components. Artificial intelligence templating predicted implanted femoral and tibial size within two sizes in 85.9% and 84.4% of cases, respectfully, and predicted patella size within three millimeters in 92.6% of cases. AI-generated TJA templating software appears to overestimate component sizing and for THA templating does not outperform surgeons in evaluated metrics. While such technology shows promise in aiding in the preoperative templating workflow, refinement is necessary before integration into clinical practice.

title: Diabetic retinopathy feature utilisation in 54 convolutional neural networks: A heatmap analysis.
desc: [Acta ophthalmologica] To investigate how artificial intelligence (AI) systems detect referable diabetic retinopathy (DR) from retinal photographs by analysing heatmap patterns and determining their overlap with DR features. Fifty-four AI systems were developed using 27 backbone architectures, with each implemented as both binary-referable and multi-class grading models based on the International Clinical Diabetic Retinopathy (ICDR) grading scale. Models were trained on DDR, BRSET and Kaggle datasets. After training, each model analysed 749 images with DR feature annotations, with Grad-CAM, Integrated Gradients, LIME and SHAP heatmaps generated and compared to pixel-level annotations of microaneurysms, haemorrhages, exudates, cotton wool spots, venous beading, intraretinal microvascular abnormalities and neovascularisation. All models achieved acceptable predictive performance (AUROC >0.8 for most architectures). Heatmap analysis revealed consistent attention to the central and temporal macular region. Exudates and cotton wool spots were highlighted most frequently by the heatmaps, with venous beading and neovascularisation at the disc showing poor overall coverage for binary referable classifiers. Models grading per the ICDR scale demonstrated higher coverage for all features. Substantial variability was observed between architectures, suggesting different feature detection capabilities. Interestingly, the heatmap analysis indicated that the models may be using different features to the ICDR grading scale definitions. AI models do not uniformly correlate with all DR features when detecting referable DR, limiting their predictive performance in unusual presentations. Heatmap aggregation analysis provides a scalable method for analysing model behaviour, allowing strengths and weaknesses to be assessed. These findings may help improve clinicians' trust and acceptance of AI.
